quiz.question: 1. Why is an enrollment table useful in a relational learning platform?
options: It removes the need for user identifiers
It represents the many-to-many relationship between students and courses
It guarantees every query uses an index
quiz.explanation: Students can enroll in multiple courses, and courses have multiple students. A junction table (enrollments) models this many-to-many relationship and holds relationship-specific lifecycle attributes (enrolled_at, status, expiration).

quiz.question: 2. What is the main purpose of a foreign key?
options: Guarantee the fastest possible query
Enforce a relationship with referenced data
Automatically shard a table
quiz.explanation: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity at the database layer. They ensure that child records cannot reference nonexistent parent records and prevent accidental deletion of parents with dependent children.

quiz.question: 3. Which dependency is primarily addressed by 2NF?
options: An attribute depending on only part of a composite candidate key
A query with no index
A network request that times out
quiz.explanation: Second Normal Form (2NF) requires 1NF and ensures that no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key (eliminating partial functional dependencies).

quiz.question: 4. When is embedding data in a document often useful?
options: When related bounded data is frequently read together
Whenever the data has any relationship at all
When every query must be a relational join
quiz.explanation: Embedding data within a document is ideal when the child dataset is strictly bounded (does not grow indefinitely) and is consistently read in a single operational access alongside the parent document.

quiz.question: 5. What is a significant cost of adding too many indexes?
options: Indexes eliminate unique constraints
Every insert and relevant update must maintain affected indexes
The database can no longer execute joins
quiz.explanation: Indexes are not free: every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statement must synchronously update the B-tree nodes of all corresponding indexes, consuming CPU, disk I/O, and buffer memory.

quiz.question: 6. Which PostgreSQL index type is commonly used for B-tree-supported equality, range, and ordering queries?
options: B-tree
GIN only
BRIN only
quiz.explanation: B-tree is the default and most widely used index type in PostgreSQL, supporting =, <, <=, >, >=, and ORDER BY queries efficiently in logarithmic time.

quiz.question: 7. Why does an index beginning with user_id and then status often poorly support filtering by status alone?
options: A B-tree cannot store text
The leading index column does not match that filter pattern
Composite indexes cannot contain more than two columns
quiz.explanation: B-trees are sorted by their leading column first. If a query only filters by the second column (status), the database cannot traverse the index tree hierarchy and usually resorts to a full sequential table scan.

quiz.question: 8. What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE do in PostgreSQL?
options: Only parses SQL without executing it
Executes the statement and reports actual execution statistics along with the plan
Automatically creates every missing index
quiz.explanation: While EXPLAIN only displays the optimizer's estimated plan, EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query, recording actual wall-clock execution times, memory usage, buffer hits, and actual rows processed.

quiz.question: 9. What is the difference between replication and sharding?
options: Replication maintains copies; sharding distributes data across partitions or nodes
They are identical techniques
Sharding is the process of creating SQL indexes
quiz.explanation: Replication copies the same data across multiple nodes for fault tolerance and read scaling. Sharding partitions disjoint subsets of data across different nodes to scale write capacity and memory.

scenarios.title: How do you detect and fix the infamous N+1 query problem?
scenarios.context: A course lesson page executes 1 query for the course, then 50 separate SQL queries inside a loop for each lesson's progress.
scenarios.answer: The N+1 problem occurs when an application retrieves parent records in one query and then fires N separate child queries. Fix it using: 1) SQL JOIN or `WHERE id IN (...)` batch queries; 2) In Node.js/GraphQL, use DataLoader which batches and de-duplicates keys within a single event loop tick; 3) In ORMs (Prisma, TypeORM, Hibernate), use eager loading (`include:` or `JOIN FETCH`). This reduces database round-trips from 51 to 1 or 2.

scenarios.title: Why does PostgreSQL accumulate index bloat, and how does VACUUM work?
scenarios.context: A high-write table becomes slow over time despite having appropriate indexes.
scenarios.answer: PostgreSQL uses Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC). When a row is updated or deleted, the old version is not overwritten immediately; it is marked dead. Dead tuple pointers remain in B-tree indexes until reclaimed by AUTOVACUUM. If autovacuum cannot keep up with high write frequency, index bloat occurs (indexes occupy multiple gigabytes of stale disk pages). Fix by tuning autovacuum aggressiveness, running `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or utilizing HOT (Heap-Only Tuples) optimization.

scenarios.title: How do you perform zero-downtime schema migrations on a 50M-row production table?
scenarios.context: Adding a NOT NULL column or new index to a live table without acquiring an exclusive table lock.
scenarios.answer: Never run `CREATE INDEX` or `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN NOT NULL` directly on huge production tables. 1) Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` so reads and writes continue unimpeded. 2) To add a column with a default: in modern Postgres (11+), adding a column with a constant default is instantaneous (catalog-only update). 3) For complex column rewrites, use the expand-contract pattern: add new column as nullable, backfill asynchronously in batches, deploy code that dual-writes, validate, then drop old column.

scenarios.title: When should you choose a UUID vs BIGINT Auto-Incrementing Primary Key?
scenarios.context: Deciding the primary key strategy for PrepSpaces users and submissions.
scenarios.answer: BIGINT Identity columns are 8 bytes, sequential, cache-friendly, and maintain optimal B-tree page packing (appends always land on the rightmost leaf page). Random UUIDv4 is 16 bytes, causes severe B-tree page fragmentation (random page splits across disk), and bloats memory buffers. If you need client-generated unguessable IDs, use UUIDv7 (time-ordered sequential UUID) or ULID. They combine 128-bit uniqueness with chronological B-tree insert clustering.

scenarios.title: How do you safely cache database queries in Redis without stale read bugs?
scenarios.context: Caching course catalog responses in Redis with Cache-Aside vs Write-Through.
scenarios.answer: Use Cache-Aside with short TTLs and explicit cache invalidation. When a course is updated: 1) Commit the transaction to PostgreSQL; 2) Delete the corresponding key in Redis (`DEL course:101:summary`). Deleting is superior to updating because it prevents race conditions where an old write overwrites a newer cached value. If network partitions prevent cache invalidation, fallback TTLs (e.g. 5 minutes) guarantee bounded staleness.

scenarios.title: What are the real-world trade-offs of PostgreSQL Read Replicas vs Sharding?
scenarios.context: PrepSpaces reads are 90% of traffic, writes are 10%.
scenarios.answer: Do not shard for read-heavy workloads! Sharding introduces immense operational complexity (distributed queries, two-phase commits, rebalancing). Instead, deploy 2 to 3 PostgreSQL Read Replicas with streaming replication behind PgBouncer. Direct write queries (INSERT/UPDATE) to the primary node, and route read queries (SELECT) to replicas. Address replication lag (typically <50ms) using session sticky routing (read-your-own-writes).
